summary:
LunaNav is a web application that turns complex NASA data into fast, intuitive lunar landing site evaluations. It combines real JPL Horizons ephemeris data, NASA LOLA terrain elevation, and NAIF SPICE orientation kernels to show; for any site and date; exact Sun and Earth positions relative to the terrain horizon, sunlight windows, solar power potential, and Earth communication access.

Four validated south pole candidates are pre-loaded with support for custom coordinates. An interactive 3D Moon, first-person observer view, side-by-side site comparison, and an explainable Relative Landing Site Suitability Index let planners assess trade-offs in seconds. Libration, terrain obstruction, and slope hazards are all accounted for. No value is fabricated or estimated without clear labelling.

LunaNav bridges the gap between expert tools like JPL Horizons and the rapid scenario comparison that agile mission planning demands.
details:
LunaNav queries JPL Horizons in real time to retrieve the Sun and Earth's exact azimuth and elevation at a user-selected lunar site and date, then layers NASA LOLA terrain elevation data to compute the actual terrain horizon at that location; not a smooth geometric approximation. NAIF SPICE kernels provide scientifically accurate lunar orientation including libration. From those inputs the application calculates terrain-aware sunlight windows, solar panel power output, and Earth communication access, aggregating them into an explainable Relative Landing Site Suitability Index where every sub-score and weight is visible so the ranking is auditable rather than a black box.

The interface renders an interactive 3D Moon at true selenographic coordinates, a first-person observer view showing the Sun and Earth above the real terrain skyline, timeline charts, and side-by-side site comparison tables. Four validated south pole candidates are pre-loaded alongside support for any custom coordinate. A planner can switch sites or dates and see updated assessments within seconds; compressing a workflow that previously required navigating JPL Horizons, Moon Trek, and spreadsheets separately.

The intended impact is to support agile mission planning when hardware delays or launch windows force teams to quickly re-evaluate alternatives, while also serving educators and the public by making south pole orbital geometry tangible without specialist knowledge.

Built with React, TypeScript, Three.js, and React Three Fiber on the frontend and Python, Django, NumPy, SciPy, Astropy, SpiceyPy, Rasterio, and PyProj on the backend, the key creative decision was going beyond raw ephemeris output to determine whether a Sun or Earth direction actually clears the measured terrain horizon at each specific site. When data is unavailable the system labels results as lower confidence rather than substituting invented values.
